analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in Gulf Oil Company against Bernard. Mr. Duck, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, this case is before you on a writ of certiori, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The grant of certiori is limited only to the issue respecting communications. The issue in the case is whether the District Court can enter a monitoring order recommended by the manual when potential abuses of the class action device have actually taken place. The Fifth Circuit held that such an order could not be entered, that it was a prior restraint and therefore unconstitutional. Before getting into the facts, I would like to briefly state our position. Our position is that under Rule 23, the District Court has a unique responsibility to monitor the actions of the parties before it, to protect the interest of absentees, to ensure compliance with the fiduciary obligation that attorneys have to the courts in the administration of justice. We submit to the court that in this case, the District Court properly exercised his discretion under Rule 23, and more importantly, he properly accommodated the First Amendment rights of all parties in a fair and equitable manner. Mr. Duck, is the actual order that was entered in the record here somewhere? Mr. Duck, it is, Your Honor. It's on page 124 of the Joint Appendix. Thank you. The facts in this case are very simple. The action was commenced on May 18, 1976 as a class action. The plaintiffs sought to represent a group of employees, present and former employees, at the employer's Port Arthur Refinery. They also sought to represent a group of applicants for employment nationwide without restrictions to geographic location. The applicants, the plaintiffs in this case, are being represented by three members associated with the Legal Defense Fund and two private attorneys, Ms. Morrison and Mr. Cotton. Now, one month prior to the commencement of this action, the employer in this case entered into a conciliation agreement with the EEOC and the OEO. And that agreement provided for back pay awards to about 616 employees at the plant. It's important for the court to know that the group of individuals who were going to receive conciliation benefits was much smaller than the plaintiff's proposed class. At the time the employer was served with the complaint, already 430 of the 616 individuals entitled to conciliation benefits had received those benefits. So there was only about 180 people left to sign up. At the time the employer was served, it voluntarily suspended contact with all potential class members. And the reason for this is because under Rule 23E, the employer felt that by settlement it might be interpreted to be approved by the court. And the employer wanted to wait until the action got before the court and the court could get control of the litigation. Now, four days after suit, just four days after suit, a meeting was called by respondents and attended by three of their attorneys. When you say after suit, do you mean after the filing of the complaint? Mr. Justice Rehnquist, that's right. In that meeting, as we see from affidavits of opposing counsel, beginning that are in the appendix on page 111, 114, and 117, it was shown that they discussed the issues in this lawsuit. They discussed the conciliation agreement. And they talked about the hazards of fair employment litigation. Now, it was disclosed to Gough by an attendee at the meeting. And Gough so reported to the court in its brief that the attorneys also stated to the group not to sign the conciliation agreement. If they had received checks from the employer, to send them back because they could recover double the amount in this by prosecuting this lawsuit. At that point in time, the employer was put in a very difficult position. It sought an interim order. Dr. Let me just be sure. Did the affidavits state that they represented they could recover twice as much in the litigation? No, it didn't, Your Honor. Where does that show up in the record, then? That shows up in our brief to the court where we represented to the court that that had taken place. And what was the source of that representation? Your Honor, this is outside the record, but one of the attendees, one of the black attendees at the meeting, voluntarily came forward and reported what took place to the employer. It was reconfirmed by the employer, but the individual who made the representations to Gough would not sign an affidavit for personal reasons. Well, what it boils down to is it's not in the record, then. Your Honor, we submit for purposes before the court, and what the district court had to look at, it was part of the record. It was in the brief. It was a representation by counsel. A representation you were unable to substantiate. Your Honor, it's our position in this case that the district court must be able to look at everything that's before him when trying to decide whether to enter such a monitoring order. He must look at the entire atmosphere. He shouldn't be required to resolve conflicts between attorneys or between positions. He shouldn't rely on a fact that isn't established as a fact. I mean, maybe there's a possibility that that might happen, but you can't really say that the record demonstrates that it did happen. Your Honor, it's really not our position. We are not here advocating, although we believe it happened, we're not advocating that the district court should resolve that conflict. We're simply saying that the totality of the situation that the district court looked at at that point in time gave him sufficient discretion to enter this order. Would you regard that as an essential part of what he would need in order to enter such an order? Mr. Justice Stevens, we don't. Should we assume it happened or not happened for purpose of deciding the case? I don't think it's essential for this court to resolve the conflict either. In other words, I think that the fact that. Then it seems to me you should not be relying on it here. We submit, Your Honor, that in fact it happened, that the district court could in fact take that into consideration. Well, but you can't submit as a fact something and say we don't have to decide whether it's a fact or not. Yes, sir. I would like to submit, Justice Stevens, that here we had a situation that the district court was looking at the fact the meeting took place, the fact that the affidavit stated certain representations or comments were made to the potential class members in attendance. At that time, these potential class members were making very basic decisions about their rights, whether to sign up in a conciliation agreement or whether to join in this lawsuit. And we think those factors weigh just as heavily as the conflict that exists between counsel as far as what this report had to do and the action he had to take. It seems to me there's quite a difference between a lawyer saying that the claim that would be filed would be for an amount twice as much as the settlement or something like that, which presumably might be an accurate description of the claim, and a statement by the lawyer that if we file such a claim, we guarantee that you will recover twice as much. And you're suggesting that they said the latter rather than the former. That is true, Your Honor. We do contend... And it's very possible that a person attending the meeting, reporting it, might not have the distinction between those two kinds of statements very clearly in mind. Your Honor, in this, it's not our position that any misrepresentation actually took place. It would be impossible to know if it was a misrepresentation if the lawsuit was tried and a final verdict was entered, whether it was... Well, should we decide the case on the assumption that there were no misrepresentations at that meeting? No, Your Honor. As I again urge the court to look at the entire circumstances that were before the district court, I submit to the court that it's not... So you're saying that some things outside the record should be treated as though they were before the district court? Mr. Justice Stevens, I submit to the court that the district courts acting in the discretion under the federal rules decide matters that are before them, but maybe not technically in the record, all the time. Motions to compel, discovery orders, all these types of matters. What kind of an affidavit would be sufficient to... In connection with... Would an information belief affidavit be all right or not? Mr. Justice White, to support the statements that the employer represented to the court? Yes. It's an affidavit that the employer had been informed by so-and-so, Mrs. Hearsay. Yes, sir. That's just what I think that that would again be appropriate for the district court to consider as far as what action he's going to take based upon his discretion. Well, but that's kind of an affidavit wasn't presented. That's true indeed, Your Honor. And we do submit that this case shouldn't turn on exactly what was said or resolving the differences between counsel in this case. But look at the total circumstances before the district court. The unique position that he was in when he saw the meeting that took place, when he saw the conflict between counsel... Well, of course, that... Even if... Even if you're... Even if you're right, that might not... That might not justify the order that was entered. Or that if... And even if you're wrong, then we... It doesn't mean that the order was bad, even, does it? Suppose we won't take your... Suppose we judge the case without this claim of misrepresentation. You don't say you've lost the case. Mr. Justice White, we certainly do not. And the reason for that is consider the type of order that was entered here. This was not an enter that suppressed communication. This order simply monitored what took place in that class action setting. It didn't say you couldn't speak because the order specifically exempted a number of types of communications. Suppose in this case... Suppose in this case a counsel had thought that something he wanted to send out was constitutionally protected. And he then sent it out. And then he knew that the order supposedly required that he summarize it, at least, and notify the court that he had sent it out. Suppose he had done that. Would the court of appeals have then held that that counsel's constitutional rights have been violated? Mr. Justice White, it's our position. I know, but what did the court of appeals hold? Did it also invalidate the order to the extent that it required reporting to the court a communication that counsel sent out because he thought it was constitutionally protected? Mr. Justice White, apparently it did it and validated the entire order. It held that the entire order, when they looked at it, was a prior restraint of First Amendment freedoms and was unconstitutional. But there was a provision for Senate that counsel would not have been in contempt if he had thought any statement he thought protected. If he sent it out, he would have been in contempt if he hadn't reported it afterwards. That's true, Mr. Justice White. The exemption said this, that any counsel or party may make a constitutionally protected statement to the potential class members. His only thing he had to do was report it five days later. So this exception really ate up the rule. And it might come to mind, well, didn't that destroy the purpose of this order? Well, the rule actually was that he asserted it was constitutionally protected, not that it was in fact constitutionally protected. Exactly, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, but he asserted it. And once he asserts it under the exemption, it is our position that very free communications can take place. Now, it might come to mind immediately, well, what was the purpose of the order if he could make these kind of communications? And I submit to the court, the purpose of the order was to monitor and detect. It wasn't to suppress. It allowed the judge... Do you think the Fifth Circuit held that that kind of an order would be a prior restraint? I think they did, Your Honor, in this case. They held that this was a prior restraint of First Amendment freedoms. And we think this is a particularly inappropriate case to hold the prior restraint doctrine applicable. We're talking about ongoing litigation, and the courts enter orders all the time affecting the basic First Amendment rights of parties and attorneys during ongoing litigation. I was told this morning to be here at 10 o'clock and to speak for only 30 minutes. It might have been I could explain my position better this afternoon after more thought, or that I could speak better to you for an hour. I could explain my position better, but the administration of justice requires limitations upon my rights and upon rights of counsel. And that's the kind of right we're looking at here, is the protection of the ongoing administrative process. Well, are you saying, are you suggesting that there aren't any constitutionally protected communications in a piece of ongoing litigation? The District Court apparently thought there might be. Mr. Justice White, it's our position that when you have to resolve the right of the District Court to administer his proceeding, that the constitutional rights of parties and their attorneys become lesser. They must bow to that kind. It's like Cox v. Louisiana, which extended that right even outside the courtroom, where you said picketing could be limited outside the courtroom. It's like the Supreme Court's own Rule 7, which says that clerks cannot discuss matters that are pending before the court, even after they've left the court. In the Getter's case, though, we did say that there was, at least in the federal system, a right of a client to discuss a matter with his attorney. That's right, Mr. Justice Rehnquist. In this order, specifically allowed the attorney to consult his client. It even allowed potential class members to consult the attorney if the potential class member wanted to. What it really restricted and what it really looked at was the ex parte attempt by an attorney to contact the potential class member. And even then they could have done it if they asked to do so under the exception. It was constitutionally protected. All they had to do was report it to the court five days later. We submit that because of this, it's inappropriate to apply labels to this situation. Will you say if they had asked to do so? As I had read the order, they didn't even have to ask to do so. They simply had to report that they had, in fact, done it. Mr. Justice Rehnquist, you're correct. That is, all they had to do was assert the right. They didn't have to. There was no prior approval of the court. You do it and then report it later. That's exactly right. You would concede, I take it, that any time a rule of courts, even dealing with activities of a lawyer in litigation, imposes a prior restraint that it's something that gets a very careful examination by the courts. Mr. Chief Justice, no, our position is that especially during ongoing litigation, the court must be able to exercise control over the parties and over the council. As Mr. Justice Brennan said in Nebraska Press, the council have a fiduciary obligation not to make communications that redound to the detriment of the accused and which supports the administration of justice. And that's why we think it's particularly inappropriate to look at this as a prior restraint case. It's a balancing case. In the interest to be balanced, the court's rights to administer that case, a unique class action case. It's a case where all the parties are before the court. It's not a 23B3 case where you opt in or opt out. This is a 23B2 case for all those potential class members right before the court. Could I ask you this? This order runs both against the parties and their council, as I understand it. Mr. Justice Stevens, that's correct. Do you think the same standards apply to the court's power to monitor communications between council and potential class members as would apply to communications between class members and, say, a friend or a relative who was interested in perhaps joining the class? Mr. Justice Stevens, I'm sorry. I don't quite understand your question. Well, you pointed out that the lawyer has a special fiduciary obligation both to the court and his clients, and therefore that may justify greater monitoring of the lawyer's communications to potential clients or his clients. My question is, do you apply the same standard, for purposes of analysis in this case, to potential communications between a member of the class who is a layman and someone he may know who is a potential person who might be persuaded to join the class or join the litigation? Mr. Justice Stevens, I don't think the same standard would apply. In this case, the order did apply to both council and the parties. Right. This was pre-class certification, so there were no class members. The only people... No, but there were parties. There were multiple parties. There were six parties, yes, sir. So it applied to the six parties and to council. It didn't apply to anyone else. I'm asking, does the same standard apply to those six parties as applies to the lawyer? It does indeed, Your Honor, and the reason for that is because those parties are before the court, and they could be used indirectly to accomplish what the court was trying to prevent directly. Once you submit yourself to the jurisdiction of the court, you, too, have obligations to the administration of justice, and the court can tell you if you're going to be a witness or if you're not going to be a witness. The court can sequester you, and that certainly touches on the First Amendment rights of the parties, but we don't call that a prior restraint. We say that it's necessary in order to administer the case. Why isn't it a prior restraint? What is the source of the court? Just because the person who becomes a party to litigation, he gives up some First Amendment rights he would otherwise have, you say? Your Honor, in this case... He wants to discuss the issues of the case, give a speech, whatever it might be. You can't do that. Mr. Justice Stevens, we don't suggest that parties or counsel check their constitutional rights at the courthouse door. What we're suggesting here, and this order points out, that still free-flowing communications were allowed. A lot of contact was allowed under this order. I understand, but any time a person did give a speech or talked to a friend about the lawsuit or something, he had to summarize that and tell the court about it within five days. Yes, that's true, Mr. Justice Stevens. Yes. We contend that that is not an overbroad statement because, as the manual points out, here you're reconciling again the administration of justice, the control of the court, and the protection of those absent class members who had to make very important rights at that particular time, whether they were going to sign the conciliation agreement or whether they were going to join the lawsuit. And any misrepresentation or even inaccuracies that would be given to them at that particular time could have been extremely detrimental. Well, the order was certainly a lot broader than misrepresentation. Mr. Justice White, the order... It barred absolutely truthful communications as well. Mr. Justice White, we submit that the order did not, in fact, bar our communications. Again, I point out to the court on page 124 of the appendix that that order allowed the attorneys to speak to their clients, it allowed potential class members to speak to the attorneys, and it allowed any other communication that was constitutionally protected as long as it was reported to the court. It was not restrictive. It allowed free-flowing communications. Well, I'll just put it again. It reported to effect, or to bar, unless you were going to report it to the court, absolutely truthful communications originating with counsel to someone who was not his current client. If, Mr. Justice White, you're entirely correct in this respect, that would only be with regard to solicitation of funds or solicitation of membership. I think the court called the court's attention to... Well, would this order bar a communication, a circular, put out by, a named party to the litigation or the counsel to the named party to the litigation, putting out a circular to all potential class members, including many people who hadn't hired this lawyer, urging them not to take the settlement? Mr. Justice White, such a circular could have been distributed under this order if they claimed the constitutional right to be served. No, that isn't my question. But unless they did report it to the court, that kind of a communication would have been barred. That's correct, Mr. Justice White. That's all. The order, we believe, was very narrowly tailored to accomplish its intended purpose. It's important, I think, to look at the purpose of the order. It was to detect inaccuracies or misstatements that were sent to potential class members. Respondents urge in this case that there were other reasonable alternatives that could have been used to correct the situation. In fact, they suggest that the disciplinary procedures of the VAR Association could have been brought to bear and remedial notices could have been sent out. But that obscures the intent of this order. The intent is to find out about it. If the court can't find out about it, he can't discipline the attorney, and he cannot send out remedial notices. And because we're dealing with such a large group of people, hundreds and hundreds of people nationwide, the court's going to have to know what's going on out there. Otherwise, he can't control the litigation and protect the rights of absent class members. This court said just last term in Deposit Guarantee v. Roper, that the district court has a responsibility to protect absent class members and to protect the administration of justice by monitoring the actions of the parties before it. Mr. Duck, may I ask, suppose counsel will be the third. Constitutionally, he was entitled, and he sent something out, and then within the five days he reported it to the court. The judge looked at it and didn't like the looks of it. Obviously, counsel couldn't be held in contempt. He hadn't violated the order. What could the court do about it? Well, Mr. Justice Brennan, I think under the order, the court could do nothing. The individual complied with the order in that case. Well, I suppose the court could, if he thought it misrepresented the facts, it could send a notice of its owner. Well, yes, Mr. Justice White, that's true. Or it could permit the Gulf to or the employer to send out something. That's true, Mr. Justice White. Well, would Gulf have to get the permission of the court to send its own out? Absolutely, sir. Permission? Yes, sir. Well, suppose Gulf thought that constitutionally it was entitled to respond and sent out a response and simply advised the court and sent it out. It could do that, couldn't it? Well, Mr. Justice Brennan, the order applied to both sides. That's what I mean. You didn't have to get permission to send it out, as I understood it. Anything that you wanted to send out that you asserted, constitutionally were entitled to either side, or side, so long as it filed a copy with the court. That's true, Mr. Justice, my name is. Your Honor, it seems to be conceded, Mr. Duck, that the order, at least down to paragraph number three thereof, copies in almost high verba, the proposed order worked out in the manual. Is that correct? That's true, Mr. Justice, do it. Where does the manual model appear, if it does appear in the papers before us? In the papers? It is in the appendix, and it's attached to, it's on page 97 of the appendix. Thank you. Thank you. To please the court, regardless of what action this court takes in this case, this matter is going back to the federal district court. we submit to the court that it's going to be very important for the district court to know how to control this litigation we submit to the court that there's still a very real possibility that notices inaccurate will be sent to potential class members in this case we submit to the court there's still a real possibility that meetings will be called by both sides and we submit to the court that the discretionary power of the district court must be affirmed in order to control this type of litigation mr greenberg mr chief justice and may it please the court we submit first that the order of prohibiting communication with members of the class violates the first amendment and second that those orders were issued in violation of rule 23 of the federal rules of civil procedure but if rule 23 had by its terms provided that after the filing of a lawsuit of this kind such an order be entered it did not provide that such an order could be entered what if it did well then it would you still have a constitutional argument if it we would certainly we would still have a constitutional argument certainly but not your second argument obviously yes certainly yeah and well no we would not have the second argument but our position is that rule 23 provides only for the entry of the appropriate orders and this is not a rule 23 there'd be no class action if there were no rule 23 or its equivalent there would be no class action right and you think the constitution requires that there be a rule 23 certainly not no well then doesn't but you think a rule 23 that provided for the entry of an order such as was entered in this case would be unconstitutional yes i do at least insofar as it provided for that incidentally mr greenberg is rule 23 the source of the authority for the uh what appears at 97 from the manual it purports to be as I think there's a compelling reason for that order and a similar order to juries. It's a classical kind of thing, which is necessary for the conduct of a trial occurring right before the judge. So I think that would certainly be permitted. It is not our position that a judge has no power to enter orders governing the conduct of class actions or other litigation. A judge does have power, but there has to be some reason for it. There has to be some evidence in a case like this. There has to be a hearing and a finding. The order must be narrow. For example, in the example you gave, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, I don't think an order by the court would be upheld if it were in the terms of the manual, that you are forbidden to discuss with anyone matters tending to reflect adversely upon the administration of justice or tending to reflect adversely upon any party. That order would not be upheld, I would hope. Let me carry this one step further, Mr. Greenberg. Some judges, I think this court has never had occasion to pass on it that I'm aware of, but it is not uncommon in the trial of a case when a recess is about to occur for the judge to instruct the witness who's on the stand that during the recess he may not discuss the case with anyone, including the lawyer who is examining him, who might or might not be his attorney. These such orders have been entered with respect both to independent witnesses and party witnesses. Would you think that would be a violation of the First Amendment? Certainly. It's entirely permissible and entirely appropriate. It's not a violation. It is not a violation of the First Amendment. Quite different than this case, and as I said to Mr. Justice Rehnquist, I don't think a court would uphold under the First Amendment, an order to a witness do not discuss anything that tends to reflect adversely upon the administration of justice or misrepresents the status of the case, because a witness wouldn't understand what that meant. No one would. But an order do not discuss this with anyone while during the recess, that's, I think, conventional and would be okay. As a preliminary matter, we think it important to emphasize certain facts about the record. First, there is no evidence, no evidence that plaintiff's counsel did or said anything which would constitute violation of any rule of law or any ethical norm or abuse in any other sense. The only evidence in the record on the communications issue consists of three affidavits by plaintiff's counsel and the hand bill which they desire to circulate, which appears on the last page of plaintiff's brief. The affidavits described the meetings of plaintiff's counsel with the workers at the Gulf plant and directly contradicted the assertion, the unsworn assertion in Gulf's brief, unsworn even on the basis of information and belief. Mr. Thibodeau's affidavit on 115 and 116 of the record, which is corroborated by Ms. Morrison's affidavit, states, I did not at any time during the course of the meeting advise actual or potential class members not to accept the defendant's offer of settlement, nor did I state to the assembled group that counsel for the plaintiffs could obtain twice the amount of back pay for the class as has been offered to them under the conciliation agreement. Mr. Greenberg, the manual suggests, as I understand it at least, that an order such as this be entered promptly whether or not there's been any evidence of actual abuse. It's labeled prevention of potential abuses of class action, and it says to be promptly entered in actual and potential class action orders unless there is a parallel local rule. Our position is that the manual... And some courts have done that, haven't they now? Yes. Our position is that the manual suggests a course of action contrary to the First Amendment. Well, Mr. Greenberg, in my earlier question, and I think perhaps in the Chief Justice's question, the instruction to the witnesses who are presumably going to testify in the future or the interruption of cross-examination by a recess, no finding of fact is made that the witnesses are about to discuss testimony they've heard. It's just a kind of a hornbook instruction. Well, that is in the course of the litigation and directly before the court and is a classical kind of restraint necessary to protect the fact-finding process in the conduct of the trial. I could imagine an admonition to a witness not to discuss anything with anyone months before the trial might run afoul of this rule also. I think it's a question of the circumstances of the particular situation. But in any event, the defendants talk about the record in the case. The record is unequivocal. There's nothing in the record other than flat contradiction of the unsworn assertions in the defendant's brief. And moreover, plaintiffs' affidavits were filed in June. Goff was still submitting papers on this issue as late as July 17th, and there was ample opportunity to submit contesting or contradicting affidavits or other evidence if they had any, and they didn't. Moreover, the trial court made no finding that plaintiffs' counsel had engaged in any misrepresentation or any abuse, and indeed, on this record, it could not have made any such finding. Mr. Greenberg, you don't contend, or do you, that a finding of misrepresentation or abuse of some kind is a necessary predicate for any order of this character? Mr. Greenberg, you don't contend that an order limiting communication, which would have to be a proper order, narrowly drawn and focused, and the least restrictive order possible, has to be made upon a record of some violation of law or ethical norm or perhaps other abuse, or a clear and present danger that one is about to occur. So you take the position that there is no form of order whatsoever that can be entered more or less automatically when a class action is filed pertaining to the regulation? Communications with the class? Yeah. Not as an abstract proposition. No, I cannot think of one, and counsel for defendants haven't suggested one. Not even an order saying report to the court every time you communicate with potential members or giving just a general? Well, I would like that that is indeed in the order, in this order, along with many other things, and we suggest that A, that is burdensome, and B, has a chilling effect upon communication among laymen and between lawyer and client. And so we would say that our position is that would also be a... The members of the hope-for class were not the clients of these lawyers, were they? Well, as a matter of fact, there were six named parties and 34 formal... And there was no... The order didn't affect communications between the named parties and their counsel, did it? No, it didn't, but it affected communication between the named parties and their fellow workers. Yes, but they were nobody's clients at that time, were they?
